claims.text: The protective coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
The as-manufactured coating contains a well-dispersed network of heterophase interfaces.
Creep resistance is primarily governed by the dual-phase interface architecture.
FCC/BCC heterophase boundaries impede dislocation motion under sustained stress.
Impeded dislocation motion reduces progressive plastic deformation during creep.
A thermal treatment can coarsen or dissolve heterophase interfaces and thereby reduce their density while overall composition remains constant.
The relevant structural mediator is the density and distribution of FCC/BCC heterophase interfaces.
Heterophase interfaces generate local stress fields under sustained loading.
The local stress fields interact with and pin moving dislocations.
Dislocation pinning limits dislocation glide and rearrangement, significantly slowing creep deformation.
Under identical loading conditions, the untreated coating will show lower creep strain than a thermally treated coating with reduced interface density.
The untreated coating will show a slower plastic-deformation rate than the thermally treated coating.
The untreated coating will maintain structural integrity better than the thermally treated coating under the same loading conditions.
The proposed interface-controlled mechanism operates under continuous loading at elevated temperatures where creep is active but phase transformation does not occur.
At sufficiently high temperatures or stresses that induce phase transformations, the heterophase-interface effect may cease to dominate creep resistance.
A lack of statistically significant creep-strain or deformation-rate increase after verified interface-density reduction would falsify the governing-factor hypothesis.
